chain.g: to bring home; house; cohabit with

ety.text: From Middle English haunten (“to reside, inhabit, use, employ”), from Old French hanter (“to inhabit, frequent, resort to”), from Old Northern French hanter (“to go back home, frequent”), from Old Norse heimta (“to bring home, fetch”) or/and from Old English hāmettan (“to bring home; house; cohabit with”); both from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną (“to house, bring home”), from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“village, home”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village”).

senses.d: To inhabit or to visit frequently (most often used in reference to ghosts).
ex: A couple of ghosts haunt the old, burnt-down house.
You wrong me Sir,thus ſtill to haunt my houſe.

senses.d: To make uneasy, restless.
ex: The memory of his past failures haunted him.
The murder of Déagol haunted Gollum, and he had made up a defence.

senses.d: To stalk; to follow.
ex: The policeman haunted him, following him everywhere.
Ex's and the oh-oh-oh's, they haunt me / Like ghosts, they want me / To make 'em a-a-all / They won't let go / Ex's and oh's

senses.d: To live habitually; to stay, to remain.
ex: […]That yonder in that faithfull wilderneſſe / Huge monſters haunt,and many dangers dwell;[…]

senses.d: To accustom; habituate; make accustomed to.
ex: […]haunte thi silf to pite [or pitee].

senses.d: To practise; to devote oneself to.
ex: Leave honest pleasure, and haunt no good pastime.

senses.d: To persist in staying or visiting.
ex: I haue charg’d thee not to haunt about my doores:[…]

senses.d: A place at which one is regularly found; a habitation or hangout.
ex: The shopping mall is a popular haunt of the local teenagers in this town.
I went back the town I used to live and visited all my old haunts.

senses.d: A ghost.
A lair or feeding place of animals in the wild.

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Portuguese and Catalan espantar, Italian spaventare, French épouvanter, also Romanian înspăimânta.
Borrowed from Latin inquietāre, from inquiētus (“restless”).
Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin dēmorārī.

senses.d: Of a location, frequented by a ghost or ghosts.
ex: The hotel was haunted by a disembodied spirit.

senses.d: Obsessed (by an idea, threat, etc.).
ex: a soldier haunted by the memories of combat

senses.d: Showing a feeling of being disturbed.
ex: a haunted expression

Past participle of perturbar.

From Middle English hālen, hailen, haulen, halien (“to drag, pull; to draw up”), from Old French haler (“to haul, pull”), from Frankish *halōn (“to drag, fetch, haul”) or Middle Dutch halen (“to drag, fetch, haul”), possibly merging with Old English *halian (“to haul, drag”); all from Proto-Germanic *halōną, *halēną, *hulōną (“to call, fetch, summon”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, cry, summon”). The noun is derived from the verb.

senses.d: To transport by drawing or pulling, as with horses or oxen, or a motor vehicle.
ex: to haul logs to a sawmill

senses.d: To draw or pull something heavy.
ex: The cable used for hauling the wagons on the incline may still be seen, but several of the guiding rollers have disappeared.

senses.d: To carry or transport something, with a connotation that the item is heavy or otherwise difficult to move.
To drag, to pull, to tug.
Followed by up: to summon to be disciplined or held answerable for something.
To pull apart, as oxen sometimes do when yoked.
To steer (a vessel) closer to the wind.
ex: A veſſel ſailing as near as ſhe can to the point from which the wind blows, is ſaid to be cloſe hauled.

senses.d: Of the wind: to shift fore (more towards the bow).
ex: The wind, serving us to a desire, now hauled into the west.

senses.d: To haul ass (“go fast”).
ex: “How fast was he goin’?” / “I don’t know exactly, but he must’ve been haulin’, given where he landed.”

senses.d: An act of hauling or pulling, particularly with force; a (violent) pull or tug.
The distance over which something is hauled or transported, especially if long.
ex: Getting to his place was a real haul.
I find long-haul travel by airplane tiring.

senses.d: An amount of something that has been taken, especially of fish, illegal loot, or items purchased on a shopping trip.
ex: The robber’s haul was over thirty items.
The trawler landed a ten-ton haul.

senses.d: A bundle of many threads to be tarred.
Four goals scored by one player in a game.
ex: Four goals scored by a single player in a match can be described as a 'haul', while five goals is unofficially a 'glut'.

grp.label: to carry or transport something heavy or difficult to move
to draw or pull something heavy

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish levar, from Latin levāre. The initial /ʎ/ developed from an earlier /lj/ in root-stressed conjugations such as lieva (< Latin lĕvat), where it resulted from the diphthongization of stressed Latin short ĕ to /je/. Eventually /ʎ-/ spread to the entire verb paradigm by analogy.
